title: Bromcom - 355,051 breached accounts

title: Too Lost - 724,323 breached accounts
summary: In November 2026, an unauthorised party claimed to have obtained data from the music distributor for independent artists, Too Lost. The data contained 724k unique email addresses belonging to artists, their collaborators and fans. Too Lost advised that its investigation remains ongoing, external forensic specialists have been engaged, and measures have been taken to secure affected systems and credentials. The company is also working with advisors to coordinate communications and support for affected individuals.

title: The bleph lady: Britain’s backstreet cosmetic surgeon
summary:
Luyen Vu’s discount eye surgeries represent the dangers of an unregulated beauty industry. But for her fans, she is a folk hero

Robert Laycock, a facial plastic surgeon at Aintree University Hospital in Liverpool, first knew that something was up when a patient came to him in early 2024. She was a woman in her 40s who had undergone a blepharoplasty, a procedure that involves making an incision just below or above the eyelids and removing small amounts of skin and sometimes fat and muscle. The point of the surgery is to make the patient’s face look more youthful. This woman’s stitches, however, had started coming apart, leaving an open wound right above her eyes.

It is not unusual for botched private cosmetic surgeries to be fixed on the NHS. Laycock estimates that he sees three or four patients a year who need surgical intervention after too much tissue has been removed in a blepharoplasty. But something was different about this woman. “The surgery was done in a very odd way,” Laycock told me. The incision, he explained, had been made just beneath the eyebrow rather than on the crease of the eyelid. “[It’s] not the way that we would generally do a blepharoplasty in the UK.” He asked the woman where she’d had the work done but she was evasive and he dropped the subject.

title: ‘My brother was its first body’: would you add your corpse to Birkenhead’s pyramid of dead people?

Hundreds of people wearing hi-vis clothing are on a death march through Birkenhead Park. A burning shopping trolley leads the way, smoke grenades clog the air, and people holding traffic signs chant: “The dead don’t stop – till they reach the top.” There’s a wave of curtain-twitching from residents who look on with fear and bemusement as what looks like a psychedelic building site gone rogue marches through their beautiful recreation space. Where could they be going? The answer might shock some of them. For this crowd are on their way to build a pyramid … made of dead people.

“My brother calls it my ‘anarchist death cult,’” laughs Steve Lowe, chief engineer of L-13 Light Industrial Workshop, who is involved in running Birkenhead Day of the Dead and the People’s Pyramid. It’s an event that has taken place every year (except 2020) since 2018 in a variety of locations and was announced by Jimmy Cauty and Bill Drummond of the KLF (AKA the Justified Ancients of Mu Mu AKA K2 Plant Hire Ltd), the seminal electronic duo and experimental art provocateurs, when they returned after 23 years in 2017.

Only his facial tattoos and platform boots hint at the fact that he has been responsible for some of the most extreme works of live art of all time.

Take Self-Obliteration, which begins with a naked Athey violently brushing a long blond wig pinned to his head with blunt needles, before tearing it off, upon which blood pours down his face and on to his body. title: I tried leaving all my money to my sister. She said no – and forced me to think about who really needs it
summary:
I thought making a will would be easy. Somehow, I ended up grilling my friends about their finances

I’ve spent a lot of my life thinking about death. When I was six, my dad had a heart attack. He had been our primary caregiver – the person who took us to school, took us to play in the park and bought us takeaways (the sweet man’s skills didn’t extend to the kitchen). The day it happened, my sister and I were rushed to A&E so we could see him lying wordless in a bay in case he didn’t live. Though he did survive, he never recovered and the threat of death hung over the household. It delivered on its promise when I was 18.

Rather than feeling relief that his suffering was over and the purgatory of sickness was done, I turned to worrying incessantly about the health of my mother. Because my parents were immigrants, they had no family in Britain – no one they could ask to watch us for a couple of hours without payment, let alone look out for us after they were gone. So, just before I started secondary school, my mum asked one of my friends’ parents if she could name them as our next of kin. They said yes, but not wanting to rely on others, she continued to work hard to ensure we, as well as her family in Iraq, would have as much financial security as possible.

“Even though I was raised here,” says the Iranian-American film-maker Tanaz Eshaghian from her home in New York, “I was brought up with the understanding that there are things that you do and things that you don’t do.” Take her 2006 autobiographical feature, Love Iranian-American Style, about her experience of dating in her 20s, which was, she says, “about how I was supposed to marry a nice Iranian man and stay a virgin”. But by the time she’d graduated from Brown University in Rhode Island “that ship had sailed”, she laughs.

Since Love Iranian-American Style, she has made equally taboo-breaking documentaries about a women’s prison in Afghanistan (Love Crimes of Kabul, 2011), trans people in Iran (Be Like Others, 2008) and disabled teenagers in Pakistan (As Far As They Can Run, 2022). And with each new project, the duality of her heritage (Eshaghian emigrated to the US not long after the Iranian revolution when she was six) has spurred her to focus eastwards, closer to where she was born. “When you’ve been raised in the west you can see how similar the thinking is,” Eshaghian says of the similarities she’s found there: “the conservative thinking, the place of women, what’s allowed, what’s important”.

title: ‘When I cut these women out I feel like I’m freeing them’: the feminist collage artists taking scissors to the patriarchy
summary:
A new exhibition celebrates landmark artists who sliced up existing works to make striking new pieces. The show’s curators discuss how, in order to create, sometimes you first need to destroy

When Valerie Solanas sold her SCUM Manifesto in 1967 it was priced at 10 cents for women and $1 for men. Artist Justine Kurland considered doing something similar with her “man books”: sell them off cheap to undermine their cultural weight. But knowing that people would just flip the books for a profit, instead she took a knife to what she calls the “problem of language and history and inheritance” in photography. She went through her own library of canonical male photographers, cut up the books and made collages from the spoils. Kurland called the project SCUMB (Society for Cutting Up Men’s Books), after Solanas’s manifesto.

The same idea underpins What Rose from the Cut, a group show at Graces Mews Gallery in south London. Co-curated by Kurland, the V&A Parasol Foundation curator of women in photography Fiona Rogers, and collector Sarah Miller Meigs, the show brings together more than 40 artists working in collage, photomontage and assemblage, across three generations. All the artists share a simple aim: to make something new out of something already there. The result is no one thing: the show is erotic, sentimental, irreverent and sobering, often all at once. “There is something very specific to the idea of what it is to tear something apart,” Kurland says. “There are so many things that collage immediately does right out the door.”

title: O come, all ye faithful! Why theatres are bringing audiences on stage, from Jesus Christ Superstar to Cloud 9
summary:
A wave of shows, including High School Musical and Rent, are upping the drama by placing viewers alongside actors at the heart of the action. What are the risks and rewards?

In the socially distanced summer of 2020, Jesus Christ Superstar was staged at Regent’s Park in London for a hugely pruned audience. Like the actors, we were kept two metres apart. It was a triumphant but extremely strange experience – not least from my current perspective. I’m standing on stage at Theatre Royal Drury Lane, jostling alongside other theatregoers, watching a miraculous revival of the same production. But this time, 75 audience members have been given a spot within the scaffold-style set for the show, beneath the musicians and almost side by side with the cast. The National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles (Natsal) is the crowdpleaser of the data world. Nerds love it because of its extraordinary thoroughness. It’s one of the largest studies of sexual behaviour in the world, surveying nearly 7,000 people in the UK between the ages of 16 and 59, once a decade. Everyone else loves it because they get to talk about sex. Some of the statistics speak for themselves – among 25- to 34-year-old women, the number who say they never want children has gone up fourfold, a sad, completely understandable reflection of the outside world.

Other figures, though, are mysterious: the number of women aged 16 to 24 who are on the pill has dropped precipitously, from nearly half to less than a third. Over the same period, the online space has been flooded with information about hormonal contraception, some of it better than it has ever been – more accessible, more accurate – and some of it plain wrong. Is there strategic, funded disinformation coming from Christian fundamentalists, such as we have already seen in the abortion space, where anti-abortion activists hose money at putatively “grassroots” online influencers? Or is it a quirk of the algorithms that once you go down the rabbit hole of “has the pill made me depressed?”, you will be shown endless influencers who have experienced that very (improbable) thing? It’s hard for a young person to navigate what’s real, and it’s hard to distinguish superstition from preference.

Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnist

At its centre, receiving its world premiere, was The Travelling Violin by the jazz bassist and composer Misha Mullov-Abbado. In four movements, it’s an almost-concerto on an intimate scale. The solo violin, deftly played here by Tamsin Waley-Cohen, has the narrating role, but the writing for the nine supporting string instruments is so intricately woven that it feels like an ensemble piece. It almost seemed strange for Waley-Cohen to give a solo encore at the end, mesmerising though her playing of Nicola Matteis Jr’s A minor Fantasia was.

Mullov-Abbado’s piece has a role for jazz bass, which he played himself, and for percussion, from soft-edged shimmering to driving, grooving drums, played by Fred Thomas; the jazz sensibility of both of these leaches into the rest. Led by the violinist Julian Azkoul, the ensemble was tight, churning over the tricksy rhythmic figures of the faster movements and radiating warmth in the third, which sounded like Cole Porter reflected in a slightly warped mirror. Abdullah never explained the underlying objective to me, but I think he enjoyed how much it agitated and scared adults at the same time. title: Vaim Hotel by Jon Fosse review – not your typical ghost story

She asks him to take her away with him, to the place where they both grew up, on the boat he named after her. She wants to live with him, she tells him, even though she is married, and he has never admitted his feelings. This same man, in another section, has now died. The woman returns to her husband, and tells him he must get back with her, but he has to answer to the name she gave him when they lived together. He must also move into the home of the man she had left him for. “All was strange,” the husband admits, and decides those words should be on his tombstone. Indeed, all is – and remains – very strange to the reader: the powerlessness of these men before this woman they hardly seem to know; the randomness of the events in their lives; their spooky, dream-like surreality. But most of all: Fosse’s narrative choices that thwart easy rationalisation.

Vaim Hotel is the second volume in the Nobel laureate’s loosely connected trilogy-in-progress set in the fictional Norwegian town of Vaim. Told in Fosse’s hypnotically recursive style, in a nimble translation by Damion Searls, it is ostensibly a tale of captivity that is only a touch less disorienting than its predecessor, thanks in part to the thematic correspondences it establishes. Beckettian in its relish for the absurd and the tediously mundane, this single-sentence novel opens with a man in his 50s who, for reasons he cannot quite explain, drives to Vaim, and decides to lodge at the empty Vaim Hotel, as yet unaware that he might never leave. title: Anselm Kiefer review – Holocaust-haunted forests and a glimpse into a gigantic grave
summary:
White Cube Bermondsey, London
Kiefer asks what art means after the Holocaust – but even the vast scale of his powerfully seductive paintings can’t do justice to the gravity of his themes

When the world is falling apart, the artist retreats to the studio. It’s an old story, and Anselm Kiefer has always loved the old stories, drawing for his monumental and reliably blockbuster paintings on narrative traditions ranging from Norse mythology to German Romantic poetry. So it makes sense that an artist who has dedicated his life to the question of what art means after the end of European civilisation – which is to say, after the Holocaust – should now seek out the solitude of the studio to make sense of what’s coming.

Kiefer’s exhibition at the same gallery a decade ago had the title Walhalla, after the beer hall in the sky in which dead Vikings drink away the afterlife. Now comes the more modest (you would think) subject of the artist’s studio, depicted here in a suite of lustrous landscapes and a simple wooden cabin in the forest. Rendered in flat gold leaf, the sky in these paintings gleams like a tarnished halo in an old altarpiece, while the verdigris grass pushes roughly off the canvas. Here is the place where heaven meets the earth and is transmuted – by the alchemy of this painter’s touch – into quietly numinous paintings containing elements of both.

If you can put aside the fact that Kiefer’s own studio is a vast warehouse complex on the outskirts of Paris, these paintings present a very German vision of communion with nature. They also evoke the most famous hut in modern philosophy: the Black Forest hideaway where Martin Heidegger formulated his argument that “authentic” culture must be rooted in the native landscape. The flipside of this idea, that nature is not just a scenic backdrop to human history but a living participant in it, would have, let’s just say, consequences for German painting after 1945. Here is the challenge that Kiefer has spent his career meeting: how to paint the landscape as an unspoilt refuge from society when it is littered with mass graves?

You name it, Danny Boyle has probably directed a movie about it. He’s done zombies in 28 Days Later, astronauts hurtling towards the sun in Sunshine, a man trapped under a boulder in 127 Hours, a world without the Beatles in Yesterday and junkies in Trainspotting.

Boyle was born in Radcliffe near Manchester in 1956, and was heading towards the priesthood until, aged 14, a priest of all people talked him out of it.
